fallback.title: Your configuration
fallback.description: Assembled from the answers above. Every line below traces back to one of them.

cases.title: A simple connection
cases.description: One connection to the cluster, no failover handling, no read routing. The honest choice for work that can be retried or re-run, and the smallest thing that uses the wrapper at all.

cases.title: Survives losing one instance
cases.description: Everything stays on the primary, and when the cluster promotes a different instance the wrapper notices and reconnects. The configuration most applications actually want.

cases.title: Reads on replicas, your code says when
cases.description: Your code marks read-only work and Active Record sends it to the replica role, while the wrapper keeps the writing role pointed at the current primary. Replicas absorb read traffic without any statement inspection.

cases.title: Reads on replicas, the request decides
cases.description: Active Record's middleware routes by HTTP verb, so no application code changes. Coarser than marking work yourself — a read inside a write request still goes to the primary — and it needs no annotation to work.

cases.title: Two connections, chosen by your code
cases.description: One wrapper connection on the cluster endpoint and one on the reader endpoint. Both get the plugin chain; which one a query uses is entirely your code's decision.

cases.title: Separate write and reporting paths
cases.description: Two configurations against the same cluster, so the reporting path can run for minutes without forcing the write path to tolerate the same timeouts. The split you can already point at in your code becomes the split in your configuration.

cases.title: A read-only workload
cases.description: Pointed at the reader endpoint and pinned to readers, so a promotion never drags this connection onto the primary. The reader endpoint spreads connections across replicas for you, which is the only balancing available here.

cases.title: Writes only, always authoritative
cases.description: Pinned to the writer so no statement can ever be served by a replica. The right shape for ingest paths and for anything that reads back what it just wrote.

cases.title: Survives losing a region
cases.description: The global database failover plugin follows the write path across regions when the home region becomes unavailable. Includes surviving the loss of a single instance.

alwaysTraps: Active Record does not balance individual queries across replicas — a connection stays on whichever reader it opened. Connections are spread across readers by the reader endpoint, and, when the `initial_connection` plugin is enabled against a reader endpoint, by its `initial_connection_host_selector_strategy` (default `random`).
Verify the emitted configuration against a test cluster before production. Placeholders in angle brackets are yours to fill in.

labels.staleNotice: Your earlier answer — {answer} — is not available with the toggles you just changed. It is remembered if you switch back; pick another for now.
labels.unavailableWith: Not available with your current answers
labels.regionNeedsGlobal: Surviving the loss of a region needs an Aurora global database, so only that type can be selected.
labels.failoverNeedsCluster: Surviving the loss of an instance needs a cluster with another instance to fail over to, so this type cannot be selected.
labels.awsAuthNeedsRds: IAM and Secrets Manager authentication are RDS/Aurora features. A community database you run yourself does not support them.
labels.bgUnsupportedGlobal: AWS does not support Blue/Green deployments with RDS Proxy on Aurora global databases, and the wrapper's Blue/Green plugin does not support global databases. Use a global switchover or failover instead.
labels.bgUnsupportedMultiAzCluster: AWS Blue/Green deployments are not available for RDS Multi-AZ DB clusters (they are supported for Multi-AZ DB instance deployments).
labels.bgUnsupportedCommunity: Blue/Green deployments are an Amazon RDS/Aurora feature. A community database you run yourself cannot be set up with one.

pluginRationale.failover: Detects that the cluster promoted a different instance and reconnects to it.
pluginRationale.gdb_failover: Follows the write path to another region when the home region is unavailable.
pluginRationale.initial_connection: Resolves the cluster endpoint to a specific instance when a connection opens, and distributes connections across the cluster; a default plugin because it is helpful in the common cluster case.
pluginRationale.custom_endpoint: Tracks which instances a custom endpoint currently contains.
pluginRationale.iam: Generates and caches a short-lived IAM token in place of a password.
pluginRationale.secrets_manager: Fetches credentials from Secrets Manager and re-reads them after a rotation.
pluginRationale.kms_encryption: Encrypts and decrypts column values through AWS KMS.
pluginRationale.bg: Holds traffic through a Blue/Green switchover instead of letting it fail.

notes: The initial connection plugin is listed here because it is helpful for this deployment: it resolves the cluster endpoint to a specific instance at connect time (so a new connection made right after a failover does not land on the machine that used to be the primary) and distributes connections across the cluster's instances. It is a default plugin as of v1.0.0 precisely because it is helpful in the common cluster case; it is listed explicitly so the configuration is self-describing.

The initial connection plugin is not recommended for a custom endpoint: it is incompatible with the Aurora custom endpoint URL type, so it is left out of this configuration even though it is a default plugin.

Behind a proxy there is no cluster endpoint to resolve, so the initial connection plugin — though a default — is removed here because it is not applicable; the cluster needs a name of your choosing instead.

RDS Proxy performs its own failover and the failover plugin rejects proxy endpoints, so the failover plugin is dropped here. Surviving instance loss is handled by the proxy itself rather than by the wrapper.
Behind your own name the wrapper cannot work out how to reach individual instances, so it needs both a cluster name and a host pattern whose ? stands for the instance name.
A custom endpoint holds a subset of instances that changes over time, so the custom endpoint plugin tracks its membership.

traps: This is the cluster's read-only endpoint. Writes will fail against it — point the writing configuration at the endpoint without -ro-.

notes: List only the regions this deployment can actually reach, since the wrapper will otherwise consider instances it cannot connect to.
The plugin reconnects the connection object you are holding, so keep using the same object after a failure rather than discarding it.
Active Record hands the reconnected connection back to its pool, so the pool stays usable without a restart.

axes.label: Active Record
axes.help: The pool keys were renamed in 8.1. The wrapper supports 7.2 and later, so the builder emits whichever spelling your version accepts.

questions.title: How does your app talk to the database?
questions.body: Answer this first, because it decides whether read routing and connection pooling are configurable at all. The wrapper's plugins behave identically either way; what changes is who owns everything around them.

options.label: Through Active Record
options.hint: Active Record owns the connection pool and the reading and writing roles. You configure the wrapper inside database.yml.

options.label: Through the pg or mysql2 gem directly
options.hint: The wrapper stands in for the gem's own connection class. There is no pool and no role concept, so both are yours to build.

notes: No pool exists at this layer. One wrapper connection is one database connection; supplying a pool is your job.
Nothing probes host health, so a dead database is noticed by your driver's own socket and statement timeouts, and then by the failover plugin when a call fails.

questions.title: What does this code do with data?
questions.body: Answer for one part of your application. If an API and a nightly report job share a database, they may still deserve different configurations, so walk this once for each and treat them separately.

options.label: It reads and writes, all through one connection
options.hint: A typical CRUD service. One place to configure, mixed traffic.

options.label: It reads and writes, but heavy reading is a distinct part of the app
options.hint: You can point at the reporting or export code and it is separate from the code that writes. The two want different timeouts.

notes: Two configurations rather than one, so each gets its own timeouts and its own pool.
traps: A single timeout policy cannot serve both a sub-second API and a multi-minute report. That is the reason to split, so do not collapse them back into one entry later.

options.label: This part only reads
options.hint: A reporting service, a read API, a BI connection, an export job.

notes: One configuration entry pointed at the reader endpoint. There is no second role to declare, because nothing here writes.

options.label: This part only writes, or every statement must hit the authoritative copy
options.hint: An ingest path, or a job that writes and immediately reads back what it wrote. A slightly stale read would be a correctness bug.

notes: Reads stay on the primary by construction, so a replica can never serve a stale row to this code.

questions.title: Who decides that a unit of work is a read?
questions.body: The wrapper does not route reads for you in any mode, so this asks how your application chooses between the reader and the writer.

options.label: Nobody — keep everything on the primary
options.hint: An honest and common answer. With no replica in use this is one less moving part, and replicas stay available for other work.

options.label: My code marks its read-only work
options.blocked: This needs Active Record's roles. Talking to the gem directly, there is no role to switch to.
options.hint: You wrap read-only work in a block and Active Record sends what runs inside it to the replica.

traps: If the block never wraps the work, reads keep going to the primary and nothing warns you. Verify with logs before assuming it works.
Routing is pinned while a transaction is open, so work wrapped in one read-write transaction never reaches a replica.

options.label: The HTTP verb decides
options.blocked: This is Active Record middleware. Talking to the gem directly, there is no request to inspect.
options.hint: Active Record's middleware sends writes and anything shortly after a write to the primary, and everything else to a replica.

notes: Routing is decided per request from the HTTP verb, not per statement, so a read inside a POST still goes to the primary.
traps: Read-your-own-write is guaranteed only inside the delay window, and only for the session that wrote. Raise the delay to match your replica lag.

options.label: My code picks the connection
options.blocked: Under Active Record you would switch roles rather than hold two connections. Choose one of the role-based answers instead.
options.hint: You open one connection on the cluster endpoint and one on the reader endpoint, and choose between them yourself.

notes: Two wrapper connections, each with its own plugin chain. Which one a query uses is decided by your code alone.

questions.title: What must keep working?
questions.body: Pick the highest rung you actually need — each includes the one above it. Reaching higher than you need costs monitoring threads and configuration surface, and sometimes a different database deployment.

options.label: Nothing special — if a connection drops, my app or my user retries
options.hint: Batch jobs that can re-run, internal tools, development environments.

notes: No failover plugin, so a promotion leaves your connections pointed at a machine that is no longer the primary until something reconnects them.

options.label: One database machine dying must not take my app down
options.hint: The most common real requirement. An in-flight request can still fail once, but the application recovers by itself in seconds.

assumes: The cluster has at least one other instance to promote. With a single instance there is nothing to fail over to.
notes: The wrapper reconnects; it does not replay the statement that was running. Application-level retry stays your job.

options.label: An entire AWS region becoming unavailable must not take my app down
options.hint: A business-continuity requirement. Includes the rung above, and needs a global database, which is provisioning rather than configuration.

assumes: An Aurora global database is already provisioned across your regions.

options.label: A password in configuration
options.hint: The default. Fine to start with, and the thing most teams replace first.

options.label: Short-lived IAM tokens
options.hint: The wrapper generates and caches a token instead of using a password.

notes: Tokens are cached for `iam_expiration_sec` seconds (default `870.0`), which sits just under the 15-minute token lifetime.
assumes: IAM authentication is enabled on the cluster and the database user is mapped to an IAM role.

options.label: A central secret store
options.hint: Credentials are fetched from AWS Secrets Manager and refreshed on rotation.

notes: The secret is re-read when authentication fails, so a rotation does not need a deploy. Cached credentials otherwise refresh every `secret_expiration_sec` seconds (default `870.0`).

addons.title: Noticing a dead database
addons.body: Nothing in the wrapper probes host health, so detection is whatever your layer already does. These are the knobs that exist.

options.label: Retry idempotent queries
options.blocked: Active Record supplies this. Talking to the gem directly, retrying is your code's decision.
options.hint: Active Record retries safely retryable queries once by default.

options.label: Prod idle connections sooner
options.blocked: The keepalive key arrived in Active Record 8.1.
options.hint: Shortens the default 600 second interval so a connection broken by an idle timeout somewhere in the network is found before a request needs it.

addons.title: Connection lifetime
addons.body: How long a pooled connection may live before it is replaced.

options.label: Retire connections on a schedule
options.blocked: The max_age key arrived in Active Record 8.1. On 7.2 to 8.0 there is no equivalent.
options.hint: Connections live forever by default. Retiring them bounds how long a connection can outlive the credential it was opened with.

notes: Worth setting whenever credentials expire, so that no pooled connection outlives the token that opened it. Set it with the Active Record `max_age` pool key (shown in the emitted config).

options.label: Close idle connections sooner
options.hint: Tightens the 300 second default so an idle pool stops holding server connections.

addons.title: How much concurrency?
addons.body: The pool holds five connections by default, per process, per role.

options.label: Tens of concurrent transactions
options.hint: The default of five per pool is usually enough. Leave it alone until it is not.

options.label: Around a hundred, or more
options.hint: Size it deliberately, then multiply by your processes and by the number of roles before comparing against the database's own connection limit.

notes: Active Record documents the floor as your thread count plus the async executor plus one, so raise this with your web server's thread count rather than guessing.
Each role has its own pool, so a writing and reading pair doubles the count. Multiply by process count before comparing with the server's limit.

addons.title: Planned maintenance and version upgrades
addons.label: Keep serving through a Blue/Green switchover
addons.body: Additive, and independent of what you chose for **What must keep working?** — it is a plugin you add to whichever configuration you land on.

assumes: A Blue/Green Deployment exists and the wrapper can read its status before the switchover starts.
notes: The plugin holds traffic during the switchover instead of letting it fail, then resumes against the promoted deployment.
If you connect through an RDS Proxy, AWS requires the blue cluster to be registered with the proxy before the Blue/Green deployment is created — you cannot add the proxy afterward.

addons.title: This application connects to several databases
addons.label: Give this database its own name

notes: Not optional once a process talks to more than one cluster: without distinct names their topology caches collide and a failover in one can disturb the other.

addons.title: Certain columns must be encrypted
addons.label: Encrypt column values with AWS KMS

assumes: The metadata schema exists in the database and the application's role may read it.

addons.title: What kind of database are you using?
addons.body: Optional. Set this to have the builder emit the matching wrapper_dialect and handle discovery for that deployment. Left unspecified, no dialect is emitted and the wrapper auto-detects at connect time.

options.label: Not specified — let the wrapper detect it
options.hint: No wrapper_dialect is emitted. The safe default when you are unsure.

options.label: An Aurora global database
options.hint: A cluster that spans regions. Required for surviving the loss of a region.

options.label: An Aurora cluster (primary and replicas)
options.hint: The common Aurora deployment, in a single region.

options.label: An Aurora custom endpoint
options.hint: A named subset of a cluster's instances.

options.label: An Aurora cluster's read-only endpoint
options.hint: The -ro- endpoint. Writes will fail against it.

options.label: An RDS Multi-AZ DB cluster (3 instances)
options.hint: A managed cluster with a writer and two readers. The failover plugin supports it.

options.label: An RDS Multi-AZ DB instance (2 instances)
options.hint: A primary with a hidden standby. RDS handles the failover, so the failover plugin does not support it.

options.label: An RDS Single-AZ instance (1 instance)
options.hint: One instance, nothing to fail over to.

options.label: An RDS Proxy in front of the database
options.hint: Valid for surviving instance loss — the proxy performs its own failover, so the wrapper's failover plugin is not added (it rejects proxy endpoints).

options.label: A community MySQL or PostgreSQL database
options.hint: A database you run yourself. The AWS-specific plugins do not apply.

options.label: Your own domain name or another endpoint
options.hint: The wrapper cannot discover instances behind a name it does not manage.
